clinical_subtitle: Often called sciatica / nerve-root irritation (radicular pain) in education materials
results_header: Here’s what this might relate to
why_it_might_fit: Leg-dominant shooting pain or pins and needles with a back story is a pattern often discussed as nerve-root irritation (“sciatica”) education — not a personal diagnosis.
what_people_notice: Pain may feel worse in the calf or leg than in the back.
Pins and needles or numbness in one leg or foot can occur.
Symptoms can travel along a path down the leg.
could_also_be: Nerve-root irritation / radicular pain (“sciatica” education pattern)
Mechanical low-back pain with some leg referral (see also low-back pack)
Other nerve or soft-tissue patterns a clinician would differentiate
Urgent spinal neurological problems are why red flags are checked first
what_this_is_not: This is not automatically a problem that needs surgery.
“Disc” language carefully: discs do not “slip out” in the everyday sense.
Never treat this page as confirmation you have sciatica — a clinician confirms.
settle_expectation: Leg-dominant nerve-type pain often improves over weeks to months for many people, but new bladder/bowel/saddle symptoms, sexual dysfunction, or weakness in both legs need urgent care — not watchful waiting.
soft_flags: Progressive symptoms in one leg, spreading pain, or significant day-to-day decline — see a GP soon; physio can still help with assessment and advice when red flags are absent.
